title: Classical ciphers
Why would we want secret writing?
blocks: Alice wants to send Bob a message. Eve may read whatever crosses the communication channel.
Meet at the north gate at noon.
Can Alice make the intercepted message unintelligible to Eve while allowing Bob to recover it?
take: Start with the communication problem; the construction comes next.

title: What is cryptography?
blocks: Cryptography studies mathematical methods for protecting information in the presence of adversaries.
Cryptanalysis studies how to defeat a proposed protection under specified assumptions.
Today we focus on confidentiality: preventing an interceptor from learning the message.
take: Other goals, including authenticity and integrity, belong to later lectures.

title: Plaintext, ciphertext, algorithm, key
blocks: The transformed message sent over the channel.
The rule used to encrypt and decrypt.
The parameter that selects a particular transformation.
take: Knowing a ciphertext is different from knowing the key that produced it.

title: Encryption and decryption
blocks: Alice encrypts using a key. Bob uses the corresponding key to undo the transformation.
Eve observes the ciphertext; she should not be able to recover the message without the required secret.

title: Symmetric-key encryption
blocks: Alice and Bob share a secret key before they communicate.
All five ciphers in this lecture are symmetric-key constructions: both operations are determined by that shared key.
Distributing and protecting the key is a separate task. For now, assume Alice and Bob already share it.
take: The algorithm can be public; the key is the secret parameter.

title: A mathematical model of a cipher
blocks: Specify a plaintext space, a ciphertext space, and a key space.
\mathcal P,\quad\mathcal C,\quad\mathcal K;\qquad E_k:\mathcal P\to\mathcal C,\quad D_k:\mathcal C\to\mathcal P
Correctness means that decryption recovers every allowed plaintext:
take: We will identify these objects explicitly for each construction.

title: What does the attacker know?
blocks: Assume Eve knows the cipher algorithm, but not the particular key.
Encryptions of messages selected by Eve
take: Our main substitution and Vigenère attacks use ciphertext-only information.
source: Public-algorithm principle: Kerckhoffs, La Cryptographie Militaire (1883).

title: The alphabet as a mathematical object
blocks: Normalize examples to letters only. We use uppercase for message rows; partial substitution solutions use lowercase.
take: Removing spaces or merging letters is preprocessing, and may discard information.

title: Modulo 26: the alphabet wraps around
blocks: We represent every residue by an integer from 0 to 25.
When using indexed messages, positions start at 0. Permutation tables later explicitly use positions 1 through m.

title: Historical motivation and our route
blocks: A small offset makes hand encryption simple.
An arbitrary alphabet gives many more keys.
Change the alphabet with the key position.
Encrypt pairs using a compact square.
Rearrange positions instead of changing letters.
take: We will understand each construction before examining its limitations.

title: 01 / Shift cipher
blocks: Use one fixed offset throughout the message.
A familiar historical example is Caesar’s shift by three positions.
take: The offset is the key; the alphabet and rule are public.

title: Shift cipher: definition
blocks: There are 26 mathematical keys. The key 0 is the identity, leaving 25 nontrivial shifts.

title: Why does decryption work?
blocks: Encryption adds the same residue that decryption subtracts.

Y → A with k = 2
A → Y when we subtract 2
The equality is in the residue class ring; our displayed values are its representatives.

title: Shift example: compute the first letters
take: Compute before revealing the complete row on the next slide.

title: Shift example: finish and reverse
blocks: Apply the same subtraction to every ciphertext symbol to recover the normalized plaintext.

title: Recovering a shift key
blocks: At k = 3, HELLOWORLD is meaningful, so we stop. There are at most 26 candidate keys to try.

title: Exercise: recover the message
blocks: Find a plausible key and plaintext. Explain the evidence for your choice.
If you are told M encrypts to P, recover the key directly.
take: An answer and calculation are in the instructor guide.

title: 02 / Substitution cipher
blocks: Replace the fixed shift by an arbitrary permutation of the alphabet.
Every occurrence of one plaintext letter still receives the same ciphertext letter.
take: Historical appeal: a much larger family of secret alphabets.

title: Substitution: a bijection and its inverse
blocks: S₂₆ is the set of all alphabet permutations. The secret key σ (sigma) is one chosen permutation: a one-to-one reassignment of the 26 symbols.
Its inverse σ⁻¹ maps each ciphertext symbol back to its original plaintext symbol.
take: A one-to-one map is essential: a collision would prevent unique decryption.

title: Substitution example: use the table
blocks: B E C A U S E
W T E Q X L T
take: Decrypt W by finding it in the output row: it lies under B.

title: Counting keys and preserving patterns
blocks: Trying the entire space at one billion keys per second takes approximately 12.8 billion years.
take: A large key space rules out one simple attack; it does not rule out every attack.

title: Frequency analysis: why counting helps
blocks: A substitution changes the labels of the letters, but not their occurrence counts.
If the language has characteristic frequencies, the ciphertext inherits them under unknown labels.
source: Historical context: al-Kindi described frequency-based cryptanalysis in the 9th century.

title: A language model is a guide
blocks: These are approximate English frequencies, not exact properties of every message.
Pairs such as TH, HE, IN, ER and triples such as THE, AND, ING provide additional evidence.
take: Absence of a common pair in a short message is weak evidence, not a logical impossibility.

title: Our intercepted message
blocks: Assume English plaintext. The unknown substitution key differs from the earlier illustrative table.
We will recover the message incrementally, keeping a partial key and checking each hypothesis.
source: Ciphertext and plaintext retained from the supplied deck, slides 18–36.

title: 1 / Count letters and propose a mapping
blocks: Z is the most frequent symbol: 20/168 ≈ 0.119. English e is often frequent, so begin by testing Z → e.
Other common letters remain possible. Each proposed mapping must fit every occurrence.
take: Counts suggest hypotheses; they do not identify letters with certainty.

title: 2 / Combine pair clues to extend the key
blocks: e? occurs repeatedly; ?e does not. W has frequency 0.0476. Test W → d.
?d suggests nd or ed. If Z → e is retained, bijectivity rules out R → e; try R → n.
HE is a common pair. Test N → h and inspect the resulting plaintext.
Z → e     W → d     R → n     N → h
take: The one-to-one constraint gives logical exclusions; language frequencies rank the remaining guesses.

title: 3 / Read fragments and update the key
blocks: The fragment ne·ndhe suggests “…ne and he…”, adding C → a.
RNM becomes nh·, suggesting a vowel after h. CM becomes a·; ai is more plausible than ao. Test M → i.
take: Apply these candidates throughout the message; revise any that lead to contradictions.

title: 4 / Use familiar pairs and word patterns
take: The partly decoded HNCMF then reads ·hai·; chair proposes H → c and F → r.

title: 5 / Summarize the remaining recovery
blocks: Recognizable fragments now suggest “our friend”, “from Paris”, and “looking”. These extend the key consistently.
The remaining words—examined, empty, with, evaporation, back—supply the last observed letters. Apply each addition across the whole message.
take: The repeated trial-and-check procedure is the same; we now move to the complete plaintext.

title: The recovered message
blocks: Our friend from Paris examined his empty glass with surprise, as if evaporation had taken place while he wasn’t looking. I poured some more wine and he settled back in his chair, face tilted up towards the sun.
take: J, Q, Z are absent: 3! = 6 full substitution tables still extend the 23 observed mappings.
source: Original reference example; spacing and punctuation restored by interpretation.

title: What the attack has taught us
blocks: We combined counts, pair statistics, repeated fragments, and plausible word boundaries.
Some decisions followed from the bijection constraint; others were statistical or contextual hypotheses.
A successful reconstruction explains all observed positions with one consistent substitution.
take: Exercise: identify one logical exclusion and one probabilistic guess in the walkthrough.

title: Break / 10 minutes
blocks: We have seen how a fixed substitution preserves the language’s structure.
Next we change the substitution with position and ask which patterns remain.
take: Elapsed time: 60–70 minutes

title: 03 / Vigenère cipher
blocks: Use several shift substitutions, selected by a repeating keyword.
Repeating-key polyalphabetic methods were described by Bellaso in 1553; the familiar name is associated with Vigenère.
take: Historical objective: weaken the direct link between letter identity and frequency.

title: Vigenère: spaces and key schedule
blocks: The keyword has m letters. Its effective repeating period can be smaller, as in ABCABC.

title: Encryption example: repeat the keyword
blocks:
Plaintext   CRYPTOGRAPHY
Keyword     LUCK
Key stream  LUCKLUCKLUCK
take: Predict the first six ciphertext letters before continuing.

title: Encryption example: do the arithmetic
take: The wrap-around at i = 1 gives (17 + 20) mod 26 = 11, or L.

title: Complete the example and decrypt
blocks:
Plaintext   CRYPTOGRAPHY
Key stream  LUCKLUCKLUCK
Ciphertext  NLAZEIIBLJJI
Decryption subtracts the same aligned key value. Adding and subtracting cancel at each position.
take: R at positions 1 and 7 encrypts to L and B, because the aligned key letters differ.

title: Why does ordinary frequency analysis weaken?
blocks: A plaintext letter can be shifted in several different ways, depending on its position in the key schedule.
The aggregate histogram mixes these shifted distributions.
However, positions sharing the same key index still use one fixed shift.
take: The attack will isolate those positions instead of treating all letters as one population.

title: Cryptanalysis has two linked stages
blocks: Repeated segments; a letter-match check called the index of coincidence
Validate the combined result by decrypting the message. A plausible period alone does not identify the key.

title: Kasiski: see the repeated alignment
blocks: The highlighted THE groups begin 8 positions apart. The four-letter key KING has completed two cycles, so both groups encrypt to BUK.
take: Repeated ciphertext segments can suggest a key period; accidental repetitions are also possible.

title: Kasiski: turn repetition into a candidate length
blocks: Now consider a longer intercepted message. FVR repeats at the positions below.
take: Try key lengths 1 and 5; compare their letter-match rates next.
source: Zero-based positions. Dataset: 1,045 letters; full ciphertext in Appendix A1–A2.

title: Index of coincidence (IC): a match check
blocks: The index of coincidence, or IC, is the probability that two randomly chosen distinct positions contain the same letter.
take: This tiny example explains the counting idea; its value is not a typical English reference value.

title: What does the match rate tell us?
blocks: In English, some letters occur much more often than others. This raises the chance that two sampled letters match.
A fixed shift renames the letters without changing their counts, so it preserves the match rate.
take: These are reference values for longer texts. Short samples and different languages can vary considerably.

title: A compact formula after the intuition
blocks: For a text of N letters, let fₐ be the number of occurrences of letter a.
The numerator counts equal-letter pairs; the denominator counts all ordered pairs of distinct positions.
A program can perform this count for us. The derivation and a larger worked calculation are in the appendix.
take: Use IC as evidence about letter distributions, rather than a general security test.

title: Try five: group the same key positions
blocks: If the key repeats every five letters, reading down one colour collects letters encrypted with one fixed shift.
take: The colour labels mark key positions, not recovered key letters. The five columns each contain 209 letters.

title: Check the candidate length with IC
blocks: All five columns have English-like match rates. Together with the repeats, this supports key length 5.
take: A multiple such as 10 can also look plausible; a high IC does not uniquely determine the shortest period.

title: Recover one shift by comparing frequencies
blocks: In column 1, P occurs 27 times. If it represents E, the shift is 15 − 4 = 11, giving key letter L.
take: Try all 26 shifts and compare the whole frequency pattern. The detailed scoring method is in the appendix.

title: Finish the key and check the message
take: The coherent full plaintext supports the combined key hypothesis. Individual columns need not read as words.

title: The attack as a sequence of simple checks
blocks: Measure distances between repeated ciphertext groups.
Group aligned positions and check their IC values.
Compare each trial-decrypted distribution with English.
Does the whole message make sense?
Rejoin the columns and decrypt with LEMON.
take: Repeats → candidate length → match-rate check → shifts → readable message.

title: Break / 10 minutes
blocks: We used repetitions, letter matches, and frequency patterns to recover a repeating key.
Next we replace single-letter substitution with pairs, then rearrange positions.
take: Elapsed time: 120–130 minutes

title: 04 / Playfair cipher
blocks: A compact construction for encrypting letter pairs by hand.
Invented by Charles Wheatstone in 1854 and promoted by Lyon Playfair.
take: Historical attraction: pair substitution without carrying a huge substitution table.

title: Why substitute more than one letter?
blocks: Single-letter substitution leaves each letter’s frequency directly visible under another label.
Playfair works with digrams: pairs of distinct letters prepared from the message.
Codebooks could replace entire words or instructions, but large books were harder to distribute and protect.
take: This is polygraphic substitution; Vigenère instead changes a single-letter mapping with position.

title: Build the square: normalize the keyword
blocks: P L A Y F I R E X M
Merge J into I, remove spaces, and scan left to right, skipping any letter already entered.
These ten distinct letters occupy the first two rows of the 5 × 5 square.

title: Build the square: fill the remaining cells
blocks: Then append unused letters in order.
take: Unused letters: B C D G H K N O Q S T U V W Z. Both parties build the same square.

title: Prepare the message, one pair at a time
blocks: B and A differ; consume both.
Repeated L: consume first L; insert X.
L and O differ; consume both.
O and N differ; consume both.
Thus BALLOON becomes BA LX LO ON. Do not consume both repeated L letters when inserting the filler.

title: Preparation conventions and the gold example
blocks: If one letter remains, append X. For a repeated or final X, use Q as the alternate filler.
HIDE THE GOLD IN THE TREE STUMP
HI DE TH EG OL DI NT HE TR EX ES TU MP
Only letters within the next proposed pair trigger the repeated-letter rule.
take: Preparation can lose information; we keep it separate from the reversible pair transformation.

title: Rule 1: letters in the same row
blocks: 1. Locate P and L in row 1.
2. Move each one cell to the right.
take: Grid shading marks the input pair. Decryption moves left instead of right.

title: Rule 2: letters in the same column
blocks: 1. Locate P and I in column 1.
3. Wrap from the bottom to the top.
take: Decryption moves up; both row and column rules wrap around the square.

blocks: Keep each input row; exchange the columns.

H → B at (3,1)
I → M at (2,5)
HI → BM

Keep any filler until you have recovered all the prepared letters.

title: Why exact spelling may not be recoverable
blocks:
AXA → AX AX
AA  → AX AX
Both originals produce the same prepared text and therefore the same ciphertext.
Merging I and J also loses information. Do not automatically remove every X from a decryption.
take: The pair transformation is invertible on prepared pairs; preprocessing need not be invertible.

title: Historical usefulness and cryptanalysis
blocks: Playfair offered a practical balance between manual operation and more complex substitution; it saw military field use.
Pair and longer language patterns still survive. A computer can decrypt with candidate squares and score the results.

square → decrypt → language score
modify square → keep improvement → repeat
Random restarts help with local optima. Success depends on the message, language model, and search effort.
take: Understand the historical design goal before judging it by present-day requirements.

title: 05 / Transposition cipher
blocks: Keep letter identities unchanged and permute their positions within each block.
take: Substitution changes symbols; transposition changes where they occur.

title: Solution and security discussion
blocks: For this block size, exhaustive search is small. Candidate rearrangements can also be ranked using language patterns.
With larger blocks there are more keys, but unchanged counts remain an important structural property.

title: Compare the five constructions
take: Each construction illustrates a different relationship between a transformation and its invariants.

title: From historical alphabets to digital messages
blocks: Our hand-cipher examples first removed spaces and punctuation. That preprocessing prevented exact recovery of the original formatting.
Digital encryption operates on encoded bytes or bits and can recover the complete original representation.
The next lectures develop stronger constructions and additional security goals. These five ciphers establish the language and methods for that study.
take: Historical usefulness and present-day suitability are different questions.

title: A5 / Recovered Vigenère prose, part 1
blocks: The history of secret writing is also a history of people finding patterns. A sender may replace every letter with another symbol and hope that the message will remain hidden. Yet the habits of a language survive in surprising ways. Common letters still occur often, repeated words leave repeated shapes, and familiar phrases provide clues. A careful reader does not treat any single clue as proof. Instead the reader makes a guess, checks its consequences, and changes the guess when the evidence disagrees. Computers make this process faster but do not remove the need for a clear model of the problem.
take: Word boundaries and punctuation are editorial reconstructions, not encoded by the cipher.

title: A6 / Recovered Vigenère prose, part 2
blocks: When a short key is repeated across a long message, the same positions in the key return again and again. Splitting the message into columns can reveal a simple pattern inside each column. Enough text gives the analyst a better chance of distinguishing a useful pattern from a coincidence. The lesson is that a large number of possible keys is only one part of security. We must also ask what information remains visible and what an observer can learn from it. Good engineering starts by stating the assumptions, checking examples, and looking for ways that a system can fail. A secure design must survive careful public study rather than depend on keeping the method unknown.

title: A7 / Deriving the finite-sample IC formula
blocks: There are N(N − 1) ordered pairs of distinct positions.
For a letter a, exactly fₐ(fₐ − 1) pairs have a in both positions. These events are disjoint across letters.

title: A8 / A small IC calculation, fully worked
take: Count matching pairs; do not divide by N² when positions must be distinct.
